analytic.title: Designing Usable User Interfaces of Digital Twins: Benefits and Limitations of Applying the User Centered Design Process

meeting.title: HCSE 2026 - 11th International Working Conference on Human-Centered Software Engineering

abstract.p: The User Centered Design (UCD) process is dedicated to the design and development of systems and software focusing on their usability. Identified in the mid eighties, this process revolves around the notions of users tasks and work context, design solutions identification and evaluation of those solutions with representative users. This process is, by nature, iterative, as the goal of the evaluation is to identify areas of improvements in the solutions proposed, leading to refined and improved solutions. This process was identified in the context of computerization of human activities, i.e. transforming work with the support of computerbased automation. Digital Twins (DTs) connected to a Cyber-Physical System (CPS) (also called Physical Twin (PT)), could fall under such a computerization approach, but with specificities including: the potential critical nature of the PT; the complexity of the tasks of the operators of the PT; or the unknown tasks that new users of the DT would have to perform on it. This paper identifies challenges brought by the design, development and evaluation of User Interfaces (UIs) of DTs due to these specificities. It describes the limitations of the UCD process and presents a set of extensions to address the specific issues brought by the design and evaluation of UIs of DTs. These extensions are made concrete on the real-world case study of a DT of the electric grid in Luxembourg.

analytic.title: LivEx: Enabling Live Programming over a Distributed Execution State

monogr.title: The Art, Science, and Engineering of Programming

abstract.p:
Program comprehension is challenging when the execution state is distributed across heterogeneous platforms (e.g., CPUs, virtual machines...) or multiple languages with isolated runtimes. Developers are typically restricted to local execution views, which hinders the understanding and reasoning about global program behavior.

Existing tools such as debuggers, loggers, and live programming environments expose only local states of a single programming language. This prevents understanding how local changes affect the global state involving multiple languages. It raises two key challenges: (i) accessing a coherent global state from distributed local states, and (ii) enabling developers to reason about it effectively from their own local context.

In this paper, we extend example-based live programming to address these challenges. We introduce LivEx, a domain specific language that allows developers to specify, directly at a given place of interest in the program, not only examples but also the corresponding execution entry points and probes which allow querying information on the global state. This mechanism centralizes distributed states into a unified live view, accessible from the developer's local context.

Our implementation demonstrates that LivEx allows the construction of a coherent global view from distributed local states and supports tracking the propagation of changes across platforms and languages. We evaluate our approach by examining 1) its applicability, which we find to require a low-to-moderate amount of effort; 2) its responsiveness, which scales linearly with the number of probe elements; and 3) its expressiveness, which we find to cover various use-cases.

LivEx enables developers to access and visualize, from their local context, the impact of their work on the overall global execution state.

titleStmt.title: System Test Generation for Virtual Reality Applications using Scenario Models

analytic.title: System Test Generation for Virtual Reality Applications using Scenario Models

keywords.term: Virtual reality Interaction Testing Model-based Testing System Testing

abstract.p: Virtual Reality (VR) applications are increasingly being integrated across a wide range of domains, including surgical training and industrial marketing. However, the long-term adoption and maintenance of VR applications remain limited, particularly due to the lack of effective, systematic, and reproducible software testing approaches tailored to their unique characteristics. To address this issue, we introduce UltraInstinctVR, a novel testing approach for VR applications. Relying on predefined VR models (scenarios), it automates the generation and execution of concrete VR system tests. In our empirical evaluation, we compare UltraInstinctVR with state-of-the-art automated VR testing approaches in terms of coverage and failure detection on 10 open-source VR applications. The results show that UltraInstinctVR outperforms existing automated tools for detecting unique failures and provides valuable insights for identifying real-world bugs in VR applications.
